slides.title: An event is not permission
keyPoints: One session keeps its identity
The current mode decides what an event means
Rejected events leave the mode unchanged
slides.narration: Imagine a small import session with a Begin button and a Finish button. Pressing Finish before Begin must not claim that an import completed. The same button therefore has different meaning at different times. We need a record of the current mode and rules for changing it. A finite-state machine is a system with a fixed set of named modes and permitted changes. In this chapter the modes are idle, active, and done. The session remains the same public object while its behavior changes. Our first job is to state which events are allowed. Choosing classes comes later, after we can explain what the program must preserve.
actions: Ask whether Finish should work on a brand-new session.
Have learners name the missing information: the current mode.

question.prompt: Why is the event name alone insufficient to decide the result?
question.answer: The current mode also matters. Finish succeeds in active and is rejected in idle and done.

slides.title: Write the complete transition contract
keyPoints: Idle + begin → active
Active + finish → done
Done + reset → idle
All six other pairs reject
slides.narration: Three modes and three event values produce nine possible pairs. Only three pairs are accepted. The six rejected pairs are real requirements, not unfinished branches. A rejection returns false and preserves the current mode. An accepted event returns true and moves to the stated destination. This distinction gives us two things to verify after each event: the result and the mode. Checking only a true result could miss a transition to the wrong destination. The sample is a model of import control. It does not read a file or start a worker. If real work arrives later, its completion and failure events will need rules of their own.
actions: List the nine pairs before showing implementation.
Ask learners to identify a rejection that a happy-path test would miss.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch19.json → Rejected events are part of the model

question.prompt: How many primary cases must the original three-by-three model cover?
question.answer: Nine: three accepted transitions and six rejections. Each needs an unchanged-state or destination check.

slides.title: Start with an enum and a few branches
keyPoints: Named values represent the modes
A reference lets send update the caller’s mode
Return immediately after an accepted change
slides.narration: This complete baseline uses no class hierarchy. An enum class gives related names their own type. Mode::idle selects the idle name from Mode. The ampersand in Mode& means send receives an alias for the caller's existing mode, so assigning m changes that mode. The function compares both the mode and the event before making any change. At the end, false means none of the permitted pairs matched. The output contains only acceptance results, so predict the intermediate modes as well. This is a reasonable final design for a small controller. We will add State objects only when behavior begins to spread across several mode-dependent operations.

Run the code, then explain why the first Finish is rejected.

question.prompt: What mode remains after the four calls?
question.answer: Idle. The rejected finish changes nothing; begin, finish, and reset complete one cycle.

slides.title: A convenient shortcut changes the protocol
keyPoints: A global reset ignores the current mode
No crash is needed for a serious bug
Compare required and actual transitions
slides.narration: Here is a tempting maintenance shortcut: let Reset always return the session to idle. That sounds helpful, but our contract permits Reset only from done. The demonstration starts in active and compares the shortcut with the required rule. Both functions compile, and neither uses invalid memory. Their printed results disagree because one accepts a forbidden event. This is a design bug with visible behavior, not a C++ syntax error. As timeout handling, cleanup, and status messages grow, the same mode rules may get copied into several functions. State objects can group behavior by mode so a maintainer can review the active-mode rules together.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Start idle; accept begin only from idle.
Accept finish only from active and reset only from done.
Reject other state/event pairs without mutation.
Replace old state objects only after their handlers return.
slides.narration:
A session with three permitted transitions. Each state returns a proposed next state. Session owns the current state and commits the replacement after the call completes. Returning no pointer is an ordinary rejected event.

Start idle; accept begin only from idle. Accept finish only from active and reset only from done. Reject other state/event pairs without mutation. Replace old state objects only after their handlers return.

Session owns exactly one live state during public calls. Rejected events preserve the current state. A state handler cannot destroy its own receiver through Session. Only declared transitions are accepted. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. An enum and switch are likely simpler for this exact three-state example. A table works especially well when transitions are data and behavior is small. State objects earn their cost when several state-specific operations or resources would otherwise be scattered.

slides.title: The problem: one session, different rules at different times
keyPoints: A local data-import session begins idle.
The simplest implementation uses an enum for the current mode and a switch for each event.
slides.narration:
A local data-import session begins idle. A begin event makes it active. A finish event is accepted only while active and moves it to done. A reset event is accepted only while done and returns it to idle. Every other event is rejected without changing the session. These rules form a finite-state machine: a system with a limited set of named states and permitted changes between them. A state is the current mode; a transition is an allowed change of mode in response to an event.

The simplest implementation uses an enum for the current mode and a switch for each event. That is a good choice for this three-state machine if behavior stays small. The difficulty appears when each state gains different begin, finish, status, timeout, and cleanup behavior, and those decisions spread across many switches. A maintainer can update one switch but forget another. Grouping behavior by state becomes useful when the behavior that belongs together is easier to review in one place. The object-based solution here shows that growth path without claiming it is the shortest solution to three transitions.

question.prompt: Why should finish be rejected before begin in this session?
question.answer: The session starts idle, so there is no active work to finish. An event is permitted according to the current state; the event name alone does not justify a transition.

slides.title: A state object supplies behavior for the current mode
keyPoints: State declares two operations: name and next.
enum class Event creates named event values whose type stays distinct from ordinary integers.
slides.narration:
State declares two operations: name and next. name describes the current mode. next receives an Event and returns either an owned proposed next state or no state for rejection. Idle, Active, and Done each implement this interface. Each class therefore gathers the rules for events received while that state is current. The Session context owns exactly one State through unique_ptr and delegates event decisions to it.

enum class Event creates named event values whose type stays distinct from ordinary integers. Event::begin uses the scope operator to select one name from that enum. A unique_ptr<State> return value expresses exclusive ownership of a proposed state. Returning nullptr means no proposed object and therefore no accepted transition. This is a contract chosen for this example. Another design could return an explicit result with accepted, rejected, or accepted-without-change cases when internal actions need to succeed without leaving a state.

slides.title: Understand the two times when choices are made
keyPoints: The compiler checks that each concrete state supplies compatible name and next overrides.
During execution, state_->next uses virtual dispatch to call the current object’s implementation.
slides.narration:
The compiler checks that each concrete state supplies compatible name and next overrides. The class declarations can announce functions before their complete definitions appear. Definitions such as Active::next use the scope operator to identify the class whose member is being defined. Defining the transition functions after all three classes are complete lets make_unique construct their destination types. Forward declarations alone would not provide enough information to allocate a complete object.

During execution, state_->next uses virtual dispatch to call the current object’s implementation. If that object is Active, the event is compared with Event::finish. A match constructs Done; a different event returns no object. make_unique creates the destination and returns its owning pointer. The proposed pointer remains local to send until the operation decides whether to commit. If allocation throws, the old state still exists and Session has not changed its pointer. That failure differs from a rejected event, which returns false normally.

slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch19.json → Do not destroy the state while its method is still running
slides.title: Do not destroy the state while its method is still running
keyPoints: A dangerous implementation lets a state call a context setter that immediately deletes the current state.
The assignment state_ = std::move(proposed) transfers ownership of the new state into Session and destroys the previously owned state.
slides.narration:
A dangerous implementation lets a state call a context setter that immediately deletes the current state. That setter may delete the very object whose member function is still executing. Some carefully restricted cases can avoid further access, but it is a fragile rule to maintain: adding a log that reads a member afterward can use a dead object. This design avoids the entire hazard. next only returns a proposal. Session waits for the virtual call to finish and then replaces state_.

The assignment state_ = std::move(proposed) transfers ownership of the new state into Session and destroys the previously owned state. std::move does not itself move bytes or call a transition; it enables the unique pointer’s move assignment. The old handler has already returned at this point. If there is no proposal, send returns false without changing state_. Session deletes copying and assignment and provides no move operation, keeping the non-null state invariant straightforward. A movable Session would need a documented rule for its moved-from state or a safe reinitialization strategy.

slides.title: Rejected events are part of the model
keyPoints: There are three states and three event values, so the primary behavior table has nine state-event combinations.
This model does not perform a real import, start a thread, or wait for a file.
slides.narration:
There are three states and three event values, so the primary behavior table has nine state-event combinations. Only three are accepted. The other six are not omissions; they are defined rejections. main checks all nine combinations while moving through the normal cycle. In idle, finish and reset are false. In active, begin and reset are false. In done, begin and finish are false. Each accepted event is followed by a state-name check, so a return value alone cannot hide a wrong destination.

This model does not perform a real import, start a thread, or wait for a file. It isolates transition logic for study. A real asynchronous import needs a rule for who sends finish and how a late completion is handled after cancellation. A generation identifier can distinguish a completion from the current run and one from an old run. Adding that protection requires a concrete asynchronous requirement; it should not be implied by a state diagram that only contains begin and finish arrows.

slides.title: State and Strategy solve different change problems
keyPoints: A strategy is a selected way to perform a task, such as choosing a sorting or compression rule.
For a tiny stable machine, a transition table or switch remains easier to scan than several classes and heap allocations.
slides.narration:
A strategy is a selected way to perform a task, such as choosing a sorting or compression rule. It is normally selected because a caller wants a different algorithm. State represents a mode governed by the object’s history and permitted events. Their class shapes can look alike because both delegate through an interface. Their contracts differ: selecting any next strategy may be acceptable, while jumping from idle to done without begin and finish would violate this session’s protocol.

For a tiny stable machine, a transition table or switch remains easier to scan than several classes and heap allocations. Choose State when state-specific behavior grows enough to justify grouping it, or when ownership of mode-specific data becomes important. The lab adds cancel only from active to idle. The key work is not adding one enum word; it is preserving the existing transitions, rejecting cancel from idle and done, and documenting what cancellation means. Testing the full expanded table reveals accidental new transitions that a single happy-path test would miss.

question.prompt: What should happen if allocation of a proposed state fails?
question.answer: The exception propagates before replacement, leaving the current owned state intact. The caller can report failure without claiming the transition completed.

slides.title: Group the rules that change together
keyPoints: Session is the stable public context
Idle, Active, and Done supply current behavior
State declares name and next
slides.narration: The context is the object that holds the changing mode. Here it is Session. It owns one State object and sends each event to that object. Idle, Active, and Done are concrete states: classes that supply the actual behavior for a mode. The shared State interface promises a name operation and a next operation. The name tells us the current mode. The next operation decides whether an event permits a destination. Notice the change in organization. Instead of searching several switches for active-mode rules, we can inspect Active. This pays off when a mode has substantial behavior or owns resources. For three tiny transitions, the enum baseline is still shorter.

question.answer: Session owns the current object. Its concrete state decides the permitted destination by implementing next.

slides.title: A proposal is not yet a committed transition
keyPoints: next returns an owning pointer or nullptr
Non-null means an accepted destination
Session checks before replacing its current owner
slides.narration: A unique_ptr is a handle that owns one object and destroys it when that ownership ends. next returns a unique_ptr<State> containing a proposed destination, or nullptr, an empty pointer, for rejection. That meaning is a rule chosen by this example. It does not mean that every state system must use a pointer to report success. Session first keeps the proposal in a local variable. If it is empty, send returns false and the current owner stays untouched. If it is present, Session may commit it. A system with accepted events that stay in the same mode would need a richer result, because empty currently means rejected.

theory.what: An owned proposal separates a transition decision from its commitment.
theory.why: The context can reject safely and control when the old object dies.
theory.invariant: An empty proposal never replaces the live current state.
theory.risk: Assigning an empty proposal destroys the current state and breaks later dereferences.

slides.title: Two choices happen at different times
keyPoints: override checks matching signatures at compilation
Virtual dispatch selects the current implementation at execution
Destination classes must be complete before construction
slides.narration: The compiler checks that the declared overrides match State's functions. A missing const or a wrong return type can be caught before the program runs. At execution, state_->next chooses the implementation belonging to the object actually owned by state_. The arrow reaches the owned object. An Active object compares the event with finish and may create Done. The definitions of next appear after all three state classes, because constructing a destination with make_unique requires a complete type. Merely announcing that Done exists is enough for some declarations, but not for constructing its full object. Static type checking and runtime selection solve different parts of the problem.

question.prompt: Why are the transition definitions placed after all concrete state declarations?
question.answer: Their make_unique calls construct destination objects, which requires complete class definitions at those call sites.

slides.title: Let the old handler finish before destruction
keyPoints: The current state remains alive throughout next
Move assignment transfers the new owner
Old-state destruction happens after the call returns
slides.narration: The most important line order is call first, replace second. While Active::next executes, Session still owns Active. The returned proposal is stored locally. Only after that call has returned does state_ = std::move(proposed) transfer the destination into Session and destroy the old state. std::move permits a move operation; it does not itself run the state transition. A risky design lets Active call a setter that deletes Active during its own member function. A later debug message that reads a member could then access an object whose lifetime ended. The chapter avoids that maintenance trap by keeping replacement outside the running handler entirely.
actions: Narrate the lifetime of Active from call entry through assignment.
Ask where a log may safely read the old object.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch19.json → Do not destroy the state while its method is still running

question.prompt: Does std::move(proposed) itself destroy the current state?
question.answer: No. The owning pointer’s move assignment performs the ownership change and destroys the previously owned state; std::move only enables that operation.

slides.title: Distinguish rejection from failure to allocate
keyPoints: Rejected event: false, same state
Construction failure: exception, old owner still present
No concurrency or real import work is implied
slides.narration: Two outcomes may leave the session unchanged, but they mean different things. If no transition is permitted, next returns an empty pointer and send returns false normally. If a permitted destination cannot be constructed, construction may throw an exception. The assignment has not happened, so the old state remains owned. The caller can distinguish these outcomes by the return path and exception path. This guarantee covers the shown transition logic. It does not roll back an external file write or protect two threads that call send at once. When extending the model into a real import service, define those additional failure and timing rules explicitly.

question.answer: The existing Active state remains owned because Session has not reached its replacement assignment.

Strategy: a selected algorithm, not an event protocol
slides.narration: The same diagram can be implemented with a switch, a table, or objects. Count the behavior that differs by mode, not just the number of mode names. A table is attractive when transitions are mostly data. State objects become useful when each mode has different work, resources, or cleanup rules. Strategy may use a similar pointer-to-interface shape, but its meaning differs. A caller selects an algorithm such as average or highest. A session's mode must follow permitted events and history. Letting a caller install Done whenever it wants would bypass this chapter's protocol. Good design review asks what changes and who has authority to make that change.
actions: Compare a compressor choice with an import completion event.
Have learners defend either the enum or object implementation for this exact small example.

question.prompt: Why would a public setState(Done) weaken this session design?
question.answer: It would let callers skip required events and install a mode without satisfying the transition contract.

comparisons.label: Enum or table
comparisons.text: Prefer when one small transition function captures all meaningful behavior.

comparisons.label: State objects
comparisons.text: Prefer when mode-specific operations or resources need to stay together.

comparisons.label: Strategy
comparisons.text: Use when a caller selects a way to perform a task, rather than progressing through a protocol.

slides.title: Diagnose the lost current state
keyPoints: Never overwrite the owner with an unchecked proposal
Rejecting finish in idle must preserve Idle
Check both results and state names
slides.narration: Suppose a review finds state_ = state_->next(event) in send. It looks compact, but it erases the rejection check. Finish in idle returns an empty owner. The assignment destroys Idle and leaves state_ empty. A later name call attempts to reach a missing object, which has undefined behavior. We should not run that invalid access merely to see what happens. We can diagnose it by following ownership and repair it by keeping the proposal local, checking it, then committing. A useful regression test first rejects finish and then checks that name still says idle. That test links an error path to later normal usability.
actions: Ask learners to explain the failure without relying on a possible crash.
Have them state the smallest regression sequence.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch19.json → Do not destroy the state while its method is still running

question.prompt: What three steps replace the unsafe one-line assignment?
question.answer: Store the proposed pointer locally; return false if it is empty; move it into state_ only after it is known to contain a destination.

slides.title: Extend the event table before the classes
keyPoints: Cancel adds three state-event cases
Keep all nine original cases
State = current mode + event rules + safe replacement
slides.narration: The extension adds cancel from active to idle. One event name creates three new pairs: cancel in idle, active, and done. Only the middle one succeeds. Keep the original nine checks, then add these three and continue through a normal begin, finish, reset cycle after cancellation. That continuation proves the extension did not leave the session unusable. In a real asynchronous import, cancellation raises a further question: what should a late finish from the cancelled run do? A run identifier may be needed to recognize stale completion. The current synchronous model does not solve that automatically. Recall State as an organization of behavior with a precise transition contract and lifetime order.
actions: Ask for all three cancel outcomes before showing the solution.
Finish with a thirty-second explanation of proposal versus commitment.

question.prompt: Why is checking only active plus cancel insufficient?
question.answer: It misses accidental acceptance in idle or done and regressions to existing transitions. Test the full expanded event table and later normal use.

graph.title: State: permitted transitions in the Session context
graph.caption: Transition arrows represent only accepted changes of current mode. Missing state/event edges mean rejection with no state change; they do not mean an unspecified behavior.
